https://english.radio.cz/babis-criticise.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Babiš criticises intelligence services over Polish territorial claims disinformation Facebook Twitter Prime Minister Andrej Babiš (ANO) has criticised Czech intelligence services for failing to inform him promptly about a disinformation campaign suggesting Poland was seeking Czech territory. Babiš said he first learned from the media about a fake social media profile purporting to belong to the Czech ambassador to Poland. The campaign also involved a fake Czech Radio website. President Petr Pavel described the operation as a deliberate provocation aimed at damaging Czech-Polish relations. He said he had no information linking the campaign to Russia, although he noted that Moscow had previously conducted similar destabilising operations. Photograph: AP View image in fullscreen Houthi rebels march during a mobilisation campaign in Sana’a on Thursday. The group’s advance and seizure of towns has come unexpectedly and fast. Photograph: AP Yemen Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthis advance along Red Sea coast Global struggle for control of Bab al-Mandab strait threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war Violence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran war Saudi Arabia shuts down oil pipeline, blaming drones from Iraq Oliver Holmes Sat 12 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 09.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nearly 50,000 people have fled a sudden advance by Houthi forces in western Yemen , with entire villages emptied and families trapped near frontline fighting with depleting food supplies, according to aid workers. Civilians in the Middle East’s poorest country have found themselves victims of a global struggle for control over one of the most important shipping routes in the world, which threatens to turn Yemen’s on-off conflict into a forever war. In a lightning advance this week , the Iran-backed Houthi militants have seized a string of towns along the Red Sea coast from forces aligned with the US- and Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed. Many fear a return to the full-scale civil war that killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine. Map of Yemen marking recent Houthi movements The UN International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday that 46,000 people had been displaced across the governates of Taiz and Hodeidah, where steep verdant mountain ridges give way to arid coastal plains. For many families, this was their second or even third time they had been forced out of their homes. Violence erupts in Yemen again: why it matters globally and how it is linked to the US-Iran war Read more A significant number of people were observed to be leaving the city with their belongings. Fighting has cut key roads, while phone lines are down in some areas. “The scale of displacement is increasing rapidly,” said Joe Lowry, IOM’s Middle East and north Africa spokesperson in Cairo. View image in fullscreen A heavily laden vehicle arrives in Sana’a as people flee frontline fighting. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA The most urgent needs were emergency shelters, cash assistance, food, drinking water, household items, healthcare and protection services. “Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,” Lowry said. “Many of those fleeing have arrived with very few belongings after leaving suddenly, due to shelling and frontline advances.” Lowry said aid workers were having to constantly reassess access, and adapt movements, as the situation changed. “It’s a highly fluid and uncertain situation marked by rapid territorial changes, population movements and growing concern among communities about further escalation,” he said. The Houthi advance has come unexpectedly and fast, particularly the fall of the strategic port city of Mocha – widely regarded as the birthplace of the global coffee trade and the eponym​ for chocolate-flavoured coffee. View image in fullscreen Residents fled the strategic port city of Mocha after Houthi strikes which destroyed civilian infrastructure. Photograph: Al Joumhouriya TV/Reuters Mohamed, 46, who left Mocha in the middle of the night, told Agence France-Presse there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the city. Another man, Mujahid Tahami, who set off for the southern government-held city of Aden, said some families had fallen victim to “looting by gangs as they tried to flee”. Others reported that they had managed to flee in time, some on motorbikes, but other family members were not so lucky and were stuck. Yemen analysts have long criticised the US and its allies for taking a security-focused approach to the country that undervalues diplomacy and development. Washington launched a campaign of drone attacks against Sunni al-Qaida militants for much of the 21st century, but did not pay significant attention to the hardline Shia Houthi insurgency until its forces claimed the capital in 2014. View image in fullscreen Houthi soldiers stand guard next to a makeshift camp for internally displaced persons (IDPs), in Sana’a on Thursday. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA By taking control of key areas this week, including islands off the coast, the anti-west Houthis hope to gain a direct presence near the Bab al-Mandab strait, a 20-mile stretch of water and vital trade and energy route that connects Asia with Europe. ​ The strait’s name is roughly translated as “the gate of tears” or “the gate of grief”, and its strong currents and winds made the passage between the Arabian peninsula and Africa’s east coast hazardous for centuries. Modern-day cargo ships have no physical issue passing through. ​But if ​the Houthis were to close the natural chokepoint, the impact on the global economy could be disastrous. Ships would have to reroute around the southern tip of Africa, adding thousands of extra nautical miles. The fighting has already contributed to the price of oil rising above $100 a barrel after weeks when it was trading closer to $80. The fighting in Yemen, as well as Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia , is the most significant violence in the country since the UN-brokered peace plan in 2022. The UN special envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, told an emergency security council meeting on Thursday that the country faced “a new and more dangerous phase of war”. “This renewed war should alarm us all,” Grundberg said. “It effectively marks the end of the relative calm that Yemen has experienced for over four years since the UN-brokered truce. It not only threatens to plunge Yemen into a prolonged and expanding war, but also risks yet again dragging the country into the wider and unresolved regional confrontation, with global repercussions.” View image in fullscreen ‘Civilians are bearing the brunt of renewed frontline warfare, airstrikes, shelling, and large-scale displacement,’ said Joe Lowry of the IOM. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA Instability in Yemen has been exploited by regional powers such as Saudi Arabia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates to fight proxy battles, and the failure to end the violence has led to the growth of powerful militias. The US-Israeli war on Iran has only heightened the tensions, with regional animosity at an all-time high. This has compounded one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. The most recent UN humanitarian report, released last month, warned that the country of 40 million was facing a deepening malnutrition crisis, with roughly half the population facing acute food insecurity nationwide. “Years of conflict, economic deterioration, displacement, climate-related shocks and regional tensions have steadily weakened livelihoods and household resilience,” the report warned. “At the same time, declining humanitarian funding and operational constraints are limiting the ability of aid organisations to provide assistance at the scale required.” On the Red Sea coast, those who escaped the latest wave of fighting had their lives, but were left in shock. “It’s a catastrophe, and the attacks are ongoing,” said Mohammed Khudairi, who fled the fighting to a displacement camp of wood-and-straw huts near the areas of Khokha. “We managed to leave, but others remain trapped there.” Explore more on these topics Yemen Houthis Internally displaced people Refugees Middle East and north Africa Humanitarian response United Nations news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://screenrant.com/four-hands-two-so.text: By Shealyn Scott Published Aug 31, 2026, 9:30 PM EDT Shealyn Scott is a Senior Writer at Screen Rant. She has been writing for the site since 2024, focused on network, reality, streaming, and classic television. A creative writer, journalist, and lover of the written word in all its forms, Shealyn enjoys deconstructing scenes from her favorite shows, using context clues and historical precedent to predict major plot points (which, due to her successful track record, has sparked rumors of clairvoyance). As an award-winning student journalist, Shealyn spent her college years advocating for the humanities while studying English Literature. Her love of storytelling propelled her to expand her degree with minors in Writing and History, believing life to be a mere collection of stories that can be framed in as many ways as a movie scene. As a Senior member of the TV Team, Shealyn treats the series she covers like books, analyzing every line, camera angle, and lighting choice. Thankfully, her personal mission statement lines up perfectly with Screen Rant: every creative work deserves just as much thought from the viewer as it received from its creator. Sign in to your ScreenRant account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google Discover Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap One of Netflix's most highly-anticipated K-dramas of the year ties back to its top star's greatest role. Nowadays, K-dramas on Netflix are a dime a dozen, and every competing streaming service has invested years in the same market. Nevertheless, the Korean film industry existed decades before it landed on Netflix's radar, and South Korean television actors became international ambassadors of culture thanks to so-called "Hallyu" waves of popularity. Even in the modern age, however, icons can be born overnight and reach international stardom with a single standout role. Without question, Song Kang is one of the most beloved actors in the industry, despite his youth. Since his 2017 debut, the fan-favorite male lead has helmed legendary series, including supernatural romance My Demon, zombie horror drama Sweet Home, and irreverent rom-com Nevertheless . Considering how many Netflix originals he's starred in, it's unsurprising that Song Kang's comeback K-drama is also streaming exclusively on the world's leading streaming service. Yet, what has caught fans by surprise is how Song Kang's newest role in Four Hands, Two Sonatas harkens back to the actor's best work to date. Four Hands, Two Sonatas Feels Like A Spiritual Successor To Song Kang's Best K-Drama Two men play piano in the Netflix K-drama Four Hands, Two Sonatas. Admittedly, Four Hands, Two Sonatas has only released two of its scheduled 12 entries, but from the moment the K-drama's first episode begins, it's abundantly clear that Netflix has something special on its hands. The coming-of-age drama opens on Song Kang's Kang Bi-o at a piano competition in Prague. Though he brings the house down with a rousing performance that leaves numerous audience members misty-eyed, the phenom has little cause for celebration, as his family is cruelly underwhelmed and critical of his playing. Whereas Kang Bi-o is technically flawless but lacks passion, he finds himself suddenly rivaled by Choi Jeong-yo (Lee Jun-young), a young prodigy who has been forced to ignore his musical inclinations in order to handle his father's crushing debt. When Jeong-yo abruptly transfers to Korea Arts High School, Bi-o is forced to confront the harsh truth that someone appears to be naturally better than him, exposing the protagonist's deep-seated insecurity. With such high stakes and emotional turmoil right off the bat, Four Hands, Two Sonatas leaves the viewer itching for the next weekly installment. Furthermore, while Song Kang's performance hits all the right notes, it's impossible to ignore how similar in tone the Netflix original feels to his true magnum opus: Navillera . In the 2021 drama, Song Kang portrays a similarly creative yet haunted young man with a fading love of ballet. Just as he begins to give up on his career, an elderly would-be ballerino begs the protagonist to make his lifelong dream come true. To an extent, Song Kang's role in Navillera feels like a Frankenstein -esque fusion of Four Hands, Two Sonatas ' two leads. Of course, there are still major narrative points of divergence that keep the K-dramas distinctive in their own right. Navillera 's focus is mainly on mortality and the many introspective lessons to be learned in old age, while Four Hands, Two Sonatas seems like a classic coming-of-age romance stretched taut with interpersonal and familial conflicts. Could Netflix's New K-Drama Be Even Better Than Navillera? Two men dancing in Navillera. From the young love subplot to the high school setting, there's an obvious argument to be made that Four Hands, Two Sonatas is more palatable for mainstream popularity. K-dramas rarely shy away from devastating twists, tear-jerking endings, and brutally honest depictions of death, but that doesn't mean viewers actively seek out stories that will make them sob. To be clear, Netflix's new K-drama is far from a breezy viewing experience, but the darkest aspects of the first two episodes don't permeate the soul in the same way Navillera does. Related 10 K-Dramas That Will Completely Take Over Your Life There are some Korean dramas so good and addictive that they will completely take over your life and leave you wishing for more episodes. Posts By Memory Ngulube Regardless of its relative obscurity, Navillera is a near-perfect K-drama , and any viewer who writes the series off is doing themselves a grave disservice. Whether you love Song Kang or have never seen him act, Navillera is the kind of show that immerses the audience in the story such that you forget the characters aren't living, breathing people. Four Hands, Two Sonatas is off to a superb start, but the series irrefutably has big shoes to fill if it hopes to claim the title as Song Kang's best K-drama. https://www.dw.com/en/us-denmark-reach-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MsdP Trump claimed that the US would take 'permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland' Image: Odd Andersen/AFP Advertisement US President Donald Trump on Friday said that the US had reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving Washington permanent military access to the Arctic island. The Danish and Greenlandic governments also announced a breakthrough in negotiations, but stressed that the agreement respected Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination. The agreement is expected to be signed next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. What does the agreement give the US? Trump said the deal would allow the United States to maintain a permanent security presence in Greenland. "At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump wrote on Truth Social. A US State Department official said the agreement gave Washington permanent access, basing and overflight rights and would prevent China and Russia from establishing military bases on the island. Trump said the US would "immediately" begin expanding its military presence in Greenland. Greenland's ice-covered minerals: No easy option To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Denmark and Greenland say? Copenhagen emphasized a different aspect of the agreement, stressing that it did not alter Greenland's constitutional status. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement recognized "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom" as well as "the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination." "I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," Frederiksen said, calling it "great for NATO and Europe." Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen also welcomed the breakthrough. "It is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States, and the Western alliance," Nielsen said. He added that the agreement recognized "Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation." Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has pressed Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States and even threatened to take it by force, insisting that the island is crucial for US security. Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly stated that the island is not for sale and have condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. What should the EU's new Arctic strategy look like? Beállítom On Thursday morning, Pope Leo XIV received Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar for a private audience in the Vatican. The Prime Minister traveled to Rome on Wednesday evening with Minister Zoltán Tarr and State Secretaries György Velkey and István Czeti, all of whom also accompanied him to the Vatican. According to a report by MTI, the first stop during the visit of the Prime Minister and his delegation was the Hungarian Chapel in St. Peter’s Basilica, from where they proceeded to the Apostolic Palace for a private audience with Pope Leo XIV. Magyar arrived at the inner courtyard of the Apostolic Palace named after St. Damasus shortly after 10:30 a.m.,where the honor guard of the Swiss Guard was lined up. The head of government was received at the entrance to the Apostolic Palace by Archbishop Peter Rajič, Prefect of the Papal Household, along with members of the papal court, who accompanied Péter Magyar and his delegation all the way to the papal library. AFP released a video of the Hungarian Prime Minister's arrival and reception. Following the private audience, the Prime Minister proceeded to the Holy See's Secretariat of State, where he held talks with Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher—known as the Vatican's Minister of Foreign Affairs—and Father Fabio Salerno, who is responsible for Hungarian affairs at the Holy See. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Holy See's Secretary of State was not present, as he is attending the UN General Assembly in New York. After the talks, the Prime Minister went to the medical clinic for the needy located next to St. Peter’s Square, accompanied by Luis Marin de San Martin, Prefect of the Dicastery for the Service of Charity, and the clinic’s head physician. The clinic was established by Pope Francis in 2015 and has since been expanded. The Hungarian Prime Minister’s visit to the Vatican began at the Hungarian Chapel located in the crypt of St. Peter’s Basilica. Péter Magyar entered the basilica through the so-called Gate of Prayer. The bronze gate is reserved for heads of state and government. The Hungarian chapel is located in the crypt of the basilica near the tombs of the Apostle Peter and the popes: Pope John Paul II consecrated it in October 1980 as a legacy of the former Hungarian pilgrim house established by St. Stephen. The Hungarian-language Mass was celebrated by Gergő Eredics, Deputy Director of the Archdiocesan Office, who emphasized that the common trait of the Hungarian saints and blesseds is that they heard God’s word and acted upon it. Father Eredics spoke about Sára Salkaházy, who was beatified in 2006, and Mária Magdolna Bódi, who was beatified in 2025. Concelebrant Viktor Zsódi, superior of the Hungarian district of the Piarist Order, spoke of the fearless witness of the Hungarian saints as he commemorated the feast day of the martyred Bishop Saint Gellért. He emphasized that St. Gellért’s motto was “Do not be afraid!” and that this was how he lived his life—he was not afraid to bear witness. Before the private audience, the Hungarian Prime Minister visited the tomb of Pope John Paul II in St. Peter’s Basilica. Péter Magyar quoted the former pope's motto of “Do not be afraid!”—saying that it has given and continues to give strength to many Hungarians during the most difficult times. In the comments section of the post, Zoltán Tanács, Minister of Science and Technology, wrote that these two simple words were what convinced him to join Tisza’s “team that brought about the change of regime.” János Nagy, Viktor Orbán’s personal secretary also left a comment under the post, writing simply, “For us too,” presumably referring to the phrase providing strength in difficult times. The Prime Minister and his delegation traveled to the Vatican on Wednesday evening after he handed over the chairmanship of the cabinet meeting to Minister Bálint Ruff. Also traveling with the Hungarian delegation were Zoltán Tarr, Minister for Social Relations and Culture; György Velkey, Parliamentary State Secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; and István Czeti, Deputy State Secretary for Ecclesiastical Affairs. “As a former Piarist student and Hungarian prime minister, it is a tremendous honor for me personally to represent our country at the Vatican before the Holy Father,” the PM said in his video message posted on Wednesday. On the occasion of the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution, Péter Magyar gave two personal gifts to Pope Leo XIV: one was a handwritten copy of Pope Pius XII’s address to the Hungarian people, broadcast on Vatican Radio on November 10, 1956, and the other was the memoirs of Prince-Primate and Cardinal Mindszenty, along with the first American edition of those memoirs, published in New York in the 1970s. “After all, the Pope is American, too. I am preparing these personal gifts and looking forward to the visit with great anticipation,” said the Prime Minister. https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026.text: 1:12 First Black female space commander gives update from international space station - video SpaceX SpaceX flight led by first Black female commander sets US speed record Four astronauts pulled up at International Space Station after eight-hour express flight led by Jessica Watkins Associated Press Thu 1 Oct 2026 23.18 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 20.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a US speed record, and that created further history with the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for Nasa after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but skies cleared enough to allow a safe liftoff from Cape Canaveral at 11.10am (1510 GMT). Seven hours and 55 minutes later, the SpaceX Dragon “Grace” capsule docked at an ISS port, setting a record for the fastest trip by a US spacecraft to the outpost. View image in fullscreen Image taken from a Nasa video shows the SpaceX capsule carrying four astronauts docking at the International Space Station. Photograph: NASA/AP In a live broadcast on Nasa TV, the capsule appeared to glide gently toward a stationary ISS as both hurtled through space at about 17,500mph (28,100 km/h). The new arrivals – Americans Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Joshua Kutryk, and Russian Sergey Teteryatnikov – floated into the space station through a pressurized vestibule and addressed colleagues on Earth late Thursday. “We are so excited to be here. This is truly a special place,” Watkins said on the Nasa livestream. “It’s amazing and kind of ironic to think that it’s such a short trip to get here because the journey to get here has been long.” View image in fullscreen Nasa astronaut Jessica Watkins waves as she departs for the launch pad at the Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Photograph: Joe Skipper/Reuters Canadian Kutryk, whose wife will give birth while he’s away, said it “feels really good” to represent his country in space, adding he was “looking forward to a good mission after some sleep. That’s what I’m gonna go do next”. The duration of the journey depends greatly on the distance between the ISS and the spacecraft at the time of launch. It took more than 30 hours for the last crew that launched from American soil to reach the station. With the late-morning launch, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with Nasa’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station after a lengthy stay in 2022. “Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed after liftoff. Although their stay at the ISS will last six months, the flight there was the quickest yet not only for Elon Musk’s company, but any American entity, including Nasa. View image in fullscreen From left, Joshua Kutryk, Luke Delaney, Jessica Watkins and Sergey Teteryatnikov at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on Thursday. Photograph: Jennifer Briggs/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Aside from Watkins, the other astronauts are newcomers to space: Delaney is a retired marine; Kutryk is a colonel in the Royal Canadian air force; and Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February. This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for Nasa, not counting 2020’s test flight. The Crew-13 designation in their mission patch pays homage to Apollo 13, the harrowing 1970 moonshot that ended with the astronauts’ safe return. View image in fullscreen SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket topped with the Dragon capsule lifts off from Cape Canaveral, Florida. Photograph: Chandan Khanna/AFP/Getty Images References to the number 13 abounded Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13”. They also carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck. “We figured it wouldn’t hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don’t need it,” Watkins said from orbit, noting they were “four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth”. Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare Read more Heather Kutryk will give birth while her husband is orbiting Earth, making him the fourth man to become a father while doing so. Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November. “A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” Nasa manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency would do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family. The Canadian Space Agency also promised to support the family. In 2004, Nasa provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit. The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehböck. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day. Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the national reconnaissance office. All this comes the same week the company’s massive Starship reached orbit for the first time. https://www.politico.eu/article/peace-is.text: Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO. The war in Gaza hasn’t figured much in campaigning for Israel’s upcoming election — despite the likelihood that Israel’s Arab minority, Palestinian by heritage, might well decide who gets to be prime minister. Israel’s Arabs make up around 20% of the electorate that will be casting ballots in the Oct. 27 parliamentary election. And thanks to complex coalition math, Arab parties might well be the ones to crown Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads a center-right opposition bloc. Advertisement Advertisement But campaigns by both the Arab parties and Jewish politicians have avoided talking about what the outcome might actually mean for Jewish-Arab relations in the region, for the possibility of a two-state solution and even for U.S. President Donald Trump’s vision for a comprehensive peace-through-prosperity deal between Israelis and the Palestinians. “The election campaign has been bizarre,” said Michael Milshtein, a retired Israeli army colonel and former head of Palestinian affairs in Israel’s military intelligence agency. “The campaign has been focused on domestic and personal issues, and on Netanyahu.” That means it hasn’t included “the very deep complicated issue of the critical relations between us and the Palestinians, and what kind of scenarios or solutions are left after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack and the Gaza War — for any kind of political settlement,” Milshtein said. But outside of Israel there’s alarm — especially among Arab leaders — over the absence of any serious debate about how to end the multi-front conflicts Israel is engaged in and what that might foretell, said HA Hellyer, a geopolitical scholar specializing in the region. “Netanyahu, or not, the Israelis are on a particular trajectory when it comes to foreign and security policies,”Hellyer told POLITICO. “Opposition politicians blame Netanyahu for Israel’s increasing diplomatic isolation and loss of support in parts of Europe and North America. But when you look at what they’re actually saying, they’re not arguing with the policies when it comes to Gaza. They support the overall settlement project in the West Bank. They support the incursion in Southern Lebanon. Their proposition is that they could have done things in a better way,” said Hellyer, who’s a fellow at Britain’s Royal United Services Institute. Advertisement Advertisement Mentions of the Gaza conflict in election campaigns have been largely limited to clashes over who was to blame for failing to prevent the Hamas attack on southern Israel, which killed more than 1,200 people. The Eisenkot-led Change bloc has focused on Netanyahu’s role in the lead-up to the Oct. 7, 2023 massacre, pointing to the failures of his government and arguing he ignored warnings of a likely big Hamas attack. But the bloc has done little to flesh out its governing policy platform. Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s campaign has sought to frame Eisenkot as an appeaser and puppet of Arab party leaders — such as Mansour Abbas, leader of the Islamist Ra’am party, and Ahmad Tibi, leader of Ta’al party — arguing he would compromise on core security issues to persuade them to join or vote with his coalition bloc after the election to give him a Knesset majority. “The lack of real content is a major problem for such a crucial election,” the Jerusalem Post lamented in an editorial this week. Few see any chance of a negotiated peace or a two-state solution any time soon. Israelis largely view international condemnation as biased, and say critics of Israel’s conduct in Gaza fail to understand what the country has to do to survive. People walk past election campaign banners in Jerusalem on Oct. 22, 2026. | John Wessels/AFP via Getty Images But at some stage or another, Israelis will have to have conversations about peace, and delaying them isn’t going to help the country reduce its deepening isolation or help repair strained ties with traditional allies, including Europeans, who are starting to impose sanctions and considering arms embargoes. Former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, a fierce Netanyahu critic, said that while there has been election debate about how successful the Gaza war has been in degrading Hamas, “it’s true that the main issue of our future with the Palestinians has been ignored.” He added: “Had I been running, I would have talked about it the whole time.” Advertisement Advertisement So why hasn’t peace been on the agenda? As Olmert sees it, the root lies in “the huge trauma of Oct. 7, along with the perception that public opinion, the mainstream, has shifted from where it was before the massacre and moved further rightward politically.” That isn’t uncommon: When Israel suffers a severe psychological blow, the political center-of-gravity habitually moves sharply to the right, favoring hawkish and nationalist positions and marginalizing more conciliatory perspectives . Olmert isn’t entirely convinced that perception is completely accurate this time, pointing out that Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party is likely to lose a significant number of its Knesset seats — from its current tally of 32 to around 20 — after next week’s elections. “Nonetheless, the perception is that general public opinion has shifted and, therefore, all of the other parties are hesitant to talk about any political process with the Palestinians or about negotiations or about a two-state solution, and so on and so forth, because they worry they’ll lose support,” Olmert said. Polls show an overwhelming majority of Jewish-Israeli backing for military action. When it comes to the conflict with Iran, Israel Democracy Institute surveys have recorded support levels as high as 93% for the initial strikes, and nearly 80% back the continuation of the war. There has also been overwhelming Jewish-Israeli support for sustaining military pressure on Hezbollah in Lebanon and for multi-front security strategies . Sven Burgsdorff, a former EU representative and ambassador to the West Bank, doesn’t subscribe to Olmert’s view, instead arguing there’s not much difference between Netanyahu and the leaders of the center-right Change bloc when it comes to Gaza or a two-state solution — something Netanyahu dismisses out of hand regularly, saying that Palestinian sovereignty is incompatible with Israel’s security . Advertisement Advertisement “Even if the right-wing Netanyahu coalition were to be replaced by the current opposition, none of its main leaders — Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Avigdor Lieberman — question the IDF’s conduct [in] the war on Gaza, nor are they supportive of the idea of Palestinian self-determination. Only Yair Golan of the Democrats and the coalition of Arab parties are in favor of that,” he said in an interview. Opposition leaders don’t criticize Netanyahu for the conduct of the Gaza war, Burgsdorff continued. Their issue with him is whether he was at fault for not protecting Israel from the 2023 attack. They also accuse him of being set on dismantling Israel’s democratic system and for having no exit strategy for his forays into broader regional conflicts. Netanyahu has made a long political career out of leveraging external crises to keep his grip on power. And even now, it would take a brave commentator to write him off and suggest that Bibi the Magician, to use one of his nicknames, has lost the magic touch. The Israeli leader has pulled off stunning turnarounds in his long political career, including in the 1990s when he beat Shimon Peres in elections held just months after the assassination of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. Olmert still hopes for a Netanyahu defeat and says if Eisenkot is installed, he might make conciliatory moves like meeting with Mahmoud Abbas, the president of Palestinian National Authority. “He won’t be able to do anything big or quickly with Bennett and Lieberman in his cabinet. Both of them are completely opposed to the idea of Palestinian sovereignty. They keep saying it all the time. ‘There will never be a Palestinian state,’” he said. “So the political space will be very limited.” But without some serious movement toward a two-state solution, Israel could risk alienating more of its traditional allies in Europe and the U.S. Advertisement Advertisement
